title: Asteroid 2026 WD Flyby Monday Misses Earth by Over One Million Miles; Diameter Still Unmeasured

content:
Asteroid 2026 WD will pass Earth on Monday, Nov. 23, at about 1:12 p.m. ET, missing the planet by roughly 1.71 million km (1.06 million miles), or 4.4 times the average distance to the Moon, according to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL close-approach data). Arrival time and miss distance are tightly constrained, but JPL lists no measured diameter. The rock's estimated 11-to-25-m (36-to-82-ft) width is inferred from brightness, and that range includes the roughly 17-to-20-m (56-to-66-ft) object that exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013.

No impact is possible on this pass if JPL's orbit solution holds: even the closest 3-sigma distance is about 1.70 million km (1.06 million miles). The useful distinction for readers is between firm numbers and assumed ones: distance and timing are firm, size is an assumption, and the size class it represents is one that surveys have barely cataloged.

Orbit From 19 Observations Fixes Flyby Timing to Six Minutes at Three Sigma

JPL's close-approach record puts closest approach at 18:13 in its TDB ephemeris time scale, which is about 1:12 p.m. ET, with a 3-sigma timing uncertainty of about six minutes. The nominal miss distance is 0.01141 au (1.71 million km, or 1.06 million miles). The 3-sigma range runs from 0.01137 to 0.01145 au, a spread of about 12,500 km (7,700 miles), or roughly 6,200 km (3,900 miles) either side of nominal. At 4.4 lunar distances, 2026 WD will clear the Moon's orbit by a wide margin, traveling at 13.9 km/s (about 31,000 mph) relative to Earth.

JPL classifies 2026 WD as an Apollo-class near-Earth asteroid, a group whose orbits cross Earth's path, with a semi-major axis larger than 1 au and a perihelion under 1.017 au. Its orbit carries it from 0.81 au (about 75 million miles) from the Sun, inside Earth's orbit, out to 3.15 au (about 293 million miles), well beyond Mars, once every 1,020 days (about 2.8 years). The orbit has an eccentricity of 0.59 and is tilted about 1 degree to the plane of the planets. Its Earth minimum orbit intersection distance is 0.0076 au (about 1.1 million km, or 0.7 million miles).

That precision rests on thin data. JPL's solution uses 19 observations spanning three days, from Nov. 16 to Nov. 19, and carries a condition code of 8 on a 0-to-9 scale, where higher means a less certain orbit. Orbital Radar describes the orbit as poorly determined, and with only three days of data the solution can shift as new observations arrive. JPL's database also lists no discoverer or discovery site for 2026 WD.

Size Estimate Swings More Than Twofold on One Unknown: Surface Reflectivity

JPL's record lists no diameter. The roughly 15 m (49 ft) figure comes from the object's absolute magnitude, H of 26.9, with an uncertainty of about 0.3, which is the brightness it would show at 1 au from both the Sun and the observer. Turning brightness into width requires the surface's reflectivity, or albedo, which is unknown for an object this new. Diameter scales with the inverse square root of albedo, so the unknown dominates the answer.

A dark surface (albedo of about 0.05) gives roughly 25 m (82 ft). A typical value near 0.14, which NASA assumes for such estimates, gives about 15 m (49 ft). A bright surface (about 0.25) gives roughly 11 m (36 ft), matching Orbital Radar's 11-to-25-m range. The largest estimate is therefore 2.2 times the smallest, which works out to roughly 11 times the volume. JPL warns that an error in assumed albedo can produce a significantly erroneous diameter, and that H itself typically carries about half a magnitude of uncertainty.

The tradeoff is measurement for assumption. Diameters for most small asteroids are estimated from brightness and distance rather than measured directly, which is why one object can carry several size labels depending on which albedo a source assumes.

Potentially Hazardous Label Tracks Survey Size Limits, Not Airburst Danger

JPL does not flag 2026 WD as a potentially hazardous asteroid. The label requires an Earth minimum orbit intersection distance of 0.05 au or less and an absolute magnitude of 22 or brighter, which roughly corresponds to 140 m (460 ft) or larger. 2026 WD meets the first test and misses the second by almost five magnitudes.

The label describes orbital proximity and a survey cutoff, not likely harm: over 99% of known potentially hazardous objects pose no impact threat over the next 100 years, and a 2023 study found H=23 fits 140 m better than the H=22 convention. The label also leaves out the size class where modern injuries occurred. The Chelyabinsk object was not detected beforehand and burst about 30 km (19 miles) up with an energy of roughly 400 to 500 kilotons of TNT. It injured 1,491 people who sought treatment, mostly from glass broken by the shock wave, damaged more than 7,200 buildings and caused losses estimated above $33 million.

One estimate puts airbursts from objects about 20 m across at roughly once every 60 years. That is context for the size class, not a forecast for 2026 WD, whose closest 3-sigma approach on this pass is still about 1.70 million km (1.06 million miles).

Why Are Small Asteroids Like 2026 WD Found Only Days Before They Pass?

Jean-Luc Margot, a University of California, Los Angeles planetary scientist, said only about 1% of near-Earth asteroids in the size range of asteroid 2026 JH2 had been observed as of May, and that it was therefore not surprising such an object was discovered only a few days before its closest approach.

Survey capacity is growing. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's survey began June 30, 2026, and the observatory is estimated to be capable of detecting 62% of near-Earth objects 140 m (460 ft) or larger, a projection that concerns objects far bigger than 2026 WD. Congress set a goal in 2005 of finding 90% of objects that size, and about 44% had been found as of January 2024. NASA's NEO Surveyor infrared telescope is scheduled to launch no earlier than September 2027.

Earlier this week, a smaller object showed the pattern. Asteroid 2026 WA, found by the University of Arizona's Mt. Lemmon Survey on Nov. 16, passed Earth at 126,400 km (78,500 miles) the next day at about 2:59 a.m. ET, roughly a third of the Moon's distance, with an ESA size estimate of 4 to 9 m (13 to 30 ft).

Planetary Radar That Could Measure Size Directly Faces Sharp Capacity Limits

Planetary radar can reveal an asteroid's size, shape and spin at resolutions near 7.5 m (25 ft). Combined with optical data, it can predict an orbit for decades. Echo strength drops off steeply with distance, so radar works only on nearby targets.

Arecibo's main telescope collapsed in December 2020, and NASA's Small Bodies Assessment Group says in its January 2026 findings that Goldstone became the only active planetary radar supporting planetary defense observations. The group says recent damage and planned maintenance of Goldstone's 70-m (230-ft) antenna will mean extended downtime and severely limit U.S. radar observations of near-Earth objects.

Can You See Asteroid 2026 WD? Not Without Large Telescopes

Orbital Radar lists 2026 WD at about magnitude 19.5 as of Nov. 22, far too faint for the naked eye or binoculars. Closest approach falls at 1:12 p.m. ET, in daylight across most of North America. Observers who want to try should use JPL's Horizons ephemeris service for a precise position at their location and time.

Distance and Timing Are Firm; Size and Long-Term Path Are Not

For Monday's flyby, the firm facts are a miss of about 1.71 million km (1.06 million miles) at about 1:12 p.m. ET, timed to within about six minutes at 3-sigma from a 19-observation orbit. The assumptions are the 11-to-25-m (36-to-82-ft) size, which rests on an unknown albedo, and the object's path beyond this pass, which a three-day arc cannot pin down. No protective action is needed for this pass. Readers get the most from the numbers by quoting the size range instead of the 15 m (49 ft) point estimate, treating the "not potentially hazardous" tag as a statement about objects 140 m (460 ft) and larger, and checking JPL's Small-Body Database record as new observations refine the orbit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is asteroid 2026 WD going to hit Earth?

No impact is predicted on this pass: JPL's closest 3-sigma distance is about 1.70 million km (1.06 million miles), and Orbital Radar reports the object is not on any impact-risk watchlist. The orbit is preliminary, so its path years from now is poorly constrained.

Could an asteroid this size hurt anyone?

Objects of a few tens of meters usually explode in the upper atmosphere, mostly harmlessly, but the roughly 20-m (66-ft) Chelyabinsk asteroid exploded over a Russian city and injured more than 1,400 people. That describes the size class, not 2026 WD, for which no impact is predicted.

What does Apollo-class mean?

Apollo asteroids are near-Earth asteroids that cross Earth's orbit, with a semi-major axis greater than 1.0 au and a perihelion distance under 1.017 au. The group is named after asteroid 1862 Apollo.

Can I see asteroid 2026 WD?

Not without large telescopes: Orbital Radar lists about magnitude 19.5 as of Nov. 22. JPL Horizons gives precise positions for a given location and time.
